subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on components of fitness, principles of training and methods of training, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain components of fitness, principles of training and methods of training for GCSE PE simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which component of fitness is the ability of a muscle or muscle group to undergo repeated contractions without tiring?
questions.explain: Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle group to keep contracting repeatedly over time without fatiguing, e.g. a rower's legs during a race.

questions.q: Which component of fitness is defined as the range of movement possible at a joint?
questions.explain: Flexibility is the range of movement available at a joint. Good flexibility improves technique and helps reduce the risk of injury.

questions.q: A tennis player watches and hits the ball smoothly. Which component of fitness links the eyes to the movement of the racket?
questions.explain: Coordination is the ability to use two or more body parts together smoothly, including hand-eye coordination when striking a ball.

questions.q: Power is best described as which combination of components?
questions.explain: Power (explosive strength) combines strength and speed, e.g. a rugby player driving off the mark or a high jumper's take-off.

questions.q: The Cooper 12-minute run test is used to measure which component of fitness?
questions.explain: The Cooper 12-minute run/walk test measures cardiovascular endurance by recording the distance covered in 12 minutes.

questions.q: The handgrip dynamometer test measures which component of fitness?
questions.explain: The handgrip (grip strength) dynamometer measures the maximal static strength of the forearm and hand muscles.

questions.q: Which test measures reaction time?
questions.explain: The ruler drop test measures reaction time. The Illinois run tests agility, the sit and reach tests flexibility, and the stork stand tests balance.

questions.q: A coach wants to test a hockey player's ability to change direction quickly. Which test is most suitable?
questions.explain: The Illinois agility test measures agility - the ability to change direction quickly - making it ideal for a hockey player.

questions.q: In the SPORT principles of training, what does the 'R' stand for?
questions.explain: SPORT stands for Specificity, Progression, Overload, Reversibility and Tedium. Reversibility means fitness is lost when training stops.

questions.q: The FITT principle is used to apply overload. What does the second 'T' stand for?
questions.explain: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type. The second T (Type) refers to the kind of training method used.

questions.q: A swimmer designs a programme that focuses on swimming-specific fitness rather than cycling. Which principle is being applied?
questions.explain: Specificity means training should match the specific demands of the activity - so a swimmer trains in the pool, working the muscles and energy systems used in swimming.

questions.q: Doing the exact same session every week can cause a performer to become bored and lose motivation. Which principle addresses this?
questions.explain: Tedium (variance) means training should be varied to prevent boredom and keep the performer motivated.

questions.q: Which training method involves a series of exercises performed at different stations?
questions.explain: Circuit training involves moving around a series of stations, each with a different exercise, and can be designed to develop many components of fitness.

questions.q: Which training method uses resistance such as free weights or machines to develop strength and muscular endurance?
questions.explain: Weight (resistance) training uses free weights or machines. High weight/low reps builds strength; low weight/high reps builds muscular endurance.

questions.q: A performer completes 30-second all-out sprints with short recoveries to boost fitness in a short time. Which method is this?
questions.explain: HIIT alternates very high-intensity work with short recovery periods, improving fitness efficiently and working the anaerobic energy system.

questions.q: Which statement about aerobic exercise is correct?
options: It is high intensity and works without oxygen
It can only last a few seconds
It is moderate intensity and uses oxygen to release energy
It always causes an immediate build-up of lactic acid
questions.explain: Aerobic exercise is lower to moderate intensity over a longer duration and uses oxygen to release energy ('with oxygen'), e.g. jogging.

questions.q: A 100m sprinter running flat out for about 10 seconds is working mainly in which way?
questions.explain: Short, high-intensity efforts like a 100m sprint are anaerobic ('without oxygen'). Energy is released without enough oxygen, producing lactic acid.

questions.q: Which of the following best helps to prevent injury when training?
options: Using correct technique and appropriate equipment, and warming up
questions.explain: Injury prevention includes warming up, using correct technique and appropriate/protective equipment, checking the environment, and not overloading too quickly.

questions.q: Which of these is a benefit of an effective warm-up before exercise?
options: It gradually increases heart rate and blood flow, and increases muscle temperature
It causes lactic acid to build up before you start
It removes the need to train
questions.explain: A warm-up gradually raises heart rate and blood flow, increases muscle temperature and range of movement, and prepares the body and mind, reducing injury risk.

questions.q: Which heart-rate range would a performer target to train in the anaerobic (higher-intensity) training zone?
questions.explain: The anaerobic training zone is roughly 80-90% of maximum heart rate (max HR = 220 - age), while the aerobic zone is about 60-80%.
